question: A Wisconsin real estate licensee's license lapsed six months ago. Under s. 452.19(1m)(a), may a licensee still pay that person a commission for a referral arrangement made before the license lapsed?
choice_a: No, once a license lapses no payment may ever be made under any circumstance
choice_b: No, only currently licensed persons may receive any commission
choice_c: Yes, because the person was licensed under ch. 452 when the referral fee arrangement was made
choice_d: Only if the payment is made within 10 days of the license lapsing
explanation: Section 452.19(1m)(a) permits payment to a person not currently licensed if that person was licensed under ch. 452 either when the commission was earned or when the referral fee arrangement was made.

question: Under s. 452.19(1m)(a), a Wisconsin licensee wants to pay a referral fee to a broker who has never held a Wisconsin license but is regularly and lawfully engaged in the real estate brokerage business in Illinois. Is this payment permitted?
choice_a: No, only brokers who have at some point held a Wisconsin license may ever be paid
choice_b: No, referral fees to any out-of-state person are always prohibited
choice_c: Only if the Illinois broker first obtains a Wisconsin reciprocal license
choice_d: Yes, because the Illinois broker is regularly and lawfully engaged in the real estate brokerage business in another state
explanation: Section 452.19(1m)(a) allows payment to a person who, though never Wisconsin-licensed, is regularly and lawfully engaged in the real estate brokerage business in another state, territory, or foreign country.

question: Section 452.19(1m)(a) prohibits a licensee from paying a fee, commission, or referral/finder's fee to an unlicensed person outside the stated exceptions. Does this prohibition apply only to payment of the full commission, or also to partial payments?
choice_a: It applies to a fee or commission "or any part thereof" -- partial payments to an ineligible unlicensed person are prohibited the same as full payments
choice_b: It applies only to payment of the full commission amount
choice_c: It applies only if the partial payment exceeds 50% of the total commission
choice_d: It applies only to payments made in cash
explanation: The statutory text bars paying a fee or commission "or any part thereof," so splitting a commission into partial payments does not avoid the prohibition.

question: A salesperson associated with a firm completes a transaction and asks the buyer to pay the salesperson directly rather than through the firm. Under s. 452.19(1m)(b), is this proper?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the salesperson reports the payment to the firm afterward
choice_b: No, because all fees, commissions, and referral/finder's fee compensation for a licensee associated with a firm must be paid to the firm
choice_c: Yes, if the buyer and salesperson agree to it in writing
choice_d: Yes, provided the amount is less than $500
explanation: Section 452.19(1m)(b) requires that when a licensee is associated with a firm, all such compensation be paid to the firm, not directly to the individual licensee.

question: A firm represents the seller in a transaction involving a 6-unit apartment building. A cooperating firm representing the buyer asks the seller's firm for a share of the commission. Does the firm-to-firm compensation prohibition in s. 452.19(3)(a) apply to this transaction?
choice_a: Yes, the prohibition applies to all real estate transactions regardless of property type
choice_b: Yes, but only if the building includes at least one owner-occupied unit
choice_c: No, because s. 452.19(3)(a) applies specifically to transactions involving residential property with 1 to 4 dwelling units
choice_d: No, because the prohibition never applies to any multi-unit property, including duplexes
explanation: Section 452.19(3)(a) is expressly scoped to residential real estate transactions involving 1-4 dwelling units; a 6-unit building falls outside that scope.

question: Under s. 452.19(4)(c), may a listing contract require the seller to pay compensation to a firm other than the listing firm?
choice_a: No, a listing contract may never mention compensation to any other firm
choice_b: Yes, without any additional condition or restriction
choice_c: Only if the Real Estate Examining Board pre-approves the listing contract's terms
choice_d: Only if that obligation is contingent on the compensation being included in the executed offer to purchase
explanation: Section 452.19(4)(c) permits a listing contract to obligate the seller to pay a non-listing firm only if that obligation is contingent on its inclusion in the executed offer to purchase.

question: A seller verbally agrees at closing to pay the buyer's firm an extra $1,000, but this agreement is never written into the offer to purchase. Under s. 452.19(4)(b), may the buyer's firm collect this payment from the seller?
choice_a: No, because a non-listing firm may not receive compensation from a party who is not its client unless the agreement to pay is documented in the executed offer to purchase
choice_b: Yes, a verbal agreement made in front of witnesses is sufficient
choice_c: Yes, as long as the buyer's firm sends written confirmation of the agreement afterward
choice_d: Yes, if the amount is under $2,500
explanation: Section 452.19(4)(b) conditions a non-listing firm's right to compensation from a non-client party on that agreement being documented in the executed offer to purchase.

question: Which materials are made admissible in evidence under s. 452.22(1), the same as originals, when properly certified by the department's secretary or designee under official seal?
choice_a: Only original signed listing contracts between a firm and a seller
choice_b: Copies of documents, orders, resolutions, and certificates made, executed, or granted by the department or board, and papers filed with the department
choice_c: Only tax records held by the Department of Revenue
choice_d: Only court filings related to a real estate dispute
explanation: Section 452.22(1) makes properly certified copies of department/board documents, orders, resolutions, certificates, and filed papers admissible the same as originals.

question: Besides certifying that a person was not the holder of a license on a specified date, what else may a chairperson's certificate under s. 452.22(2) state as prima facie evidence?
choice_a: Only the licensee's continuing education completion hours
choice_b: Only the transcript of the licensee's disciplinary hearing
choice_c: The issuance, limitation, suspension, or revocation of any license, or the reprimand of a licensee, or the filing or withdrawal of an application
choice_d: Only the dollar amount of commission the licensee earned in a given year
explanation: Section 452.22(2) extends prima facie evidentiary effect to certificates addressing license issuance, limitation, suspension, revocation, reprimand, and application filing or withdrawal, not just non-licensure.

question: Who is authorized under s. 452.22(2) to issue the certificate that serves as prima facie evidence of licensing facts?
choice_a: Any licensed broker in the state
choice_b: The clerk of the circuit court where the action is filed
choice_c: The seller's attorney of record
choice_d: The chairperson of the board or his or her designee
explanation: Section 452.22(2) vests certification authority in the chairperson of the board or his or her designee.

question: A broker performed brokerage services while duly licensed, but let the license lapse before filing a lawsuit to collect an unpaid commission. Does s. 452.20 bar the lawsuit?
choice_a: No, because s. 452.20 requires proof of licensure at the time the alleged cause of action arose, not at the time the lawsuit is filed
choice_b: Yes, the broker must be currently licensed at the time of filing suit or the action is automatically barred
choice_c: Yes, unless the broker renews the license within 10 days of filing suit
choice_d: No, because s. 452.20 does not apply to lawsuits, only administrative complaints
explanation: Section 452.20 conditions the right to sue for a commission on licensure "at the time the alleged cause of action arose," not on holding a license when suit is filed.

question: An unlicensed individual who performed acts requiring a real estate license sues in Wisconsin court to collect compensation for those acts. Under s. 452.20, what is the likely outcome?
choice_a: The action may proceed if the individual can show the client benefited from the services
choice_b: The action cannot be maintained because the person cannot allege and prove that he or she was a duly licensed broker or salesperson when the cause of action arose
choice_c: The action may proceed if the individual obtains a license before trial
choice_d: The action may proceed because s. 452.20 only applies to firms, not individuals
explanation: Section 452.20 bars maintaining a court action for a commission without alleging and proving licensure at the time the cause of action arose; an unlicensed individual cannot make that showing.

question: Under s. 452.20, is it sufficient for a plaintiff merely to allege that he or she was a duly licensed broker or salesperson, or must the plaintiff also prove it?
choice_a: A bare allegation is sufficient; proof is required only if the defendant raises the issue
choice_b: Proof is required only in jury trials, not bench trials
choice_c: The plaintiff must both allege and prove licensure at the time the cause of action arose; a bare allegation without proof is insufficient
choice_d: Neither allegation nor proof is required once the transaction has closed
explanation: Section 452.20's text requires the plaintiff to both allege and prove licensure at the relevant time, not merely assert it.

question: Under s. 452.21, is the "prima facie proof" of compensation created by proof that a person acted as a broker or salesperson conclusive, or can it be rebutted?
choice_a: It is conclusive and cannot be rebutted by any evidence
choice_b: It only applies in criminal prosecutions, never in licensing hearings
choice_c: It shifts the burden to the department to affirmatively prove no compensation was received
choice_d: It is a rebuttable presumption -- prima facie proof, not conclusive proof
explanation: "Prima facie proof" under s. 452.21 establishes a rebuttable presumption of compensation, which the person may rebut with contrary evidence.

question: Under s. 452.38(1)(a), what is the first of two conditions that must be satisfied for a licensee not to be treated as an employee of the firm for state and federal tax purposes?
choice_a: A written agreement must be entered into with the firm providing that the licensee will not be treated as an employee for federal and state tax purposes
choice_b: The licensee must complete an additional 30 hours of continuing education
choice_c: The licensee must have at least 3 years of licensed experience
choice_d: The licensee must serve as the firm's supervising broker
explanation: Section 452.38(1)(a) requires a written agreement with the firm stating the licensee will not be treated as an employee for federal and state tax purposes -- the first of two conjunctive conditions.

question: A licensee has the written independent-contractor agreement with the firm required by s. 452.38(1)(a), but only 60% of the licensee's sales-related compensation for the calendar year is directly related to brokerage services performed for the firm. Is the independent contractor test under s. 452.38(1) satisfied?
choice_a: Yes, because meeting the written-agreement requirement in par. (a) alone is sufficient
choice_b: No, because s. 452.38(1)(b) requires 75% or more of such compensation to be directly related to the brokerage services performed on behalf of the firm
choice_c: Yes, because 60% exceeds a 50% minimum threshold
choice_d: Yes, as long as the shortfall is made up in the following calendar year
explanation: Section 452.38(1)(b) sets the compensation threshold at 75% or more; 60% does not satisfy that prong even though the written agreement in par. (a) is in place.

question: Under s. 452.38(1), to qualify for independent contractor treatment, must a licensee satisfy both the written-agreement requirement in par. (a) and the 75%-compensation requirement in par. (b), or just one of the two?
choice_a: Only the written agreement in par. (a) is required
choice_b: Only the 75% compensation threshold in par. (b) is required
choice_c: Both conditions in par. (a) and par. (b) must be satisfied
choice_d: Either condition alone is sufficient, at the firm's election
explanation: Section 452.38(1) is conjunctive: both the written-agreement condition in par. (a) and the compensation-threshold condition in par. (b) must be met.

question: Under s. 452.38(1)(b), over what period is the 75% compensation threshold measured?
choice_a: On a rolling 12-month basis measured from the licensee's date of hire
choice_b: On the firm's fiscal year, whatever that firm has adopted
choice_c: Over the full life of the written agreement, regardless of calendar year
choice_d: On a calendar year basis
explanation: Section 452.38(1)(b) measures the 75% threshold on a calendar year basis.

question: Under s. 452.38(1m), does the independent contractor treatment described in s. 452.38(1) affect a licensee's obligations under ch. 108 (unemployment insurance)?
choice_a: No, s. 452.38(1m) provides that the independent contractor section does not apply to ch. 108 or rules promulgated under ch. 108
choice_b: Yes, it automatically exempts the licensee from all ch. 108 unemployment insurance contributions
choice_c: Yes, but only for licensees earning over a set commission threshold
choice_d: Yes, it requires the firm to pay double the standard ch. 108 contribution
explanation: Section 452.38(1m) carves ch. 108 (unemployment insurance) and its rules out of the independent contractor treatment in sub. (1).
source_note: hedge: Wis. Stat. 452.38(1m) -- exact statutory phrasing paraphrased from a fetched summary rather than word-for-word re-verified text; the ch. 108 carve-out itself is confirmed.

question: Under s. 452.38(2)(a), does a firm's own internal requirements affect whether a licensee who meets the conditions in sub. (1) is treated as an independent contractor?
choice_a: Yes, firm requirements always override the statutory independent contractor designation
choice_b: No, independent contractor status under sub. (1) applies notwithstanding any requirements imposed by the firm or rules promulgated by the board
choice_c: Yes, board rules can retroactively revoke independent contractor status at any time
choice_d: Yes, but only requirements the firm adopted after January 1 of that year
explanation: Section 452.38(2)(a) provides that meeting sub. (1) yields independent contractor status regardless of contrary requirements a firm imposes or rules the board promulgates.

question: Under s. 452.38(2)(b), does it matter whether the licensee is a supervising broker when determining independent contractor status under sub. (1)?
choice_a: Yes, supervising brokers can never qualify as independent contractors
choice_b: Yes, only supervising brokers may qualify as independent contractors
choice_c: No, independent contractor status under sub. (1) applies regardless of whether the licensee is a supervising broker
choice_d: Yes, supervising brokers require separate board pre-approval to qualify
explanation: Section 452.38(2)(b) makes clear that a licensee's status as a supervising broker does not change the sub. (1) independent contractor analysis.

question: A licensee is engaged as both an independent contractor and an employee for the same firm, performing different activities under each arrangement. Under s. 452.38(3), to which activities does the independent contractor treatment in sub. (1) apply?
choice_a: To all of the licensee's activities for the firm, regardless of which arrangement covers them
choice_b: To none of the licensee's activities, because dual status disqualifies the licensee entirely
choice_c: Only to activities performed outside the firm's normal business hours
choice_d: Only to the activities covered under the written agreement referenced in sub. (1)(a)
explanation: Section 452.38(3) limits sub. (1) treatment, for a dual-status individual, to the activities covered by the written agreement described in sub. (1)(a).

question: Under s. 452.14(3)(f), a salesperson associated with a firm accepts a commission directly from a party to a transaction rather than through the firm. Is this a ground for discipline?
choice_a: Yes, accepting a commission or valuable consideration from anyone except the firm with which the licensee is associated (if associated with a firm) is a disciplinary violation under s. 452.14(3)(f)
choice_b: No, salespeople may always accept commissions directly from any party to a transaction
choice_c: No, this is only a violation if the amount exceeds $5,000
choice_d: No, this is only a violation if the party is unrepresented by another licensee
explanation: Section 452.14(3)(f) makes it grounds for discipline to accept a commission or valuable consideration from anyone other than the licensee's own firm, when the licensee is associated with a firm.

question: Does the disciplinary ground in s. 452.14(3)(f) restrict a broker who operates as a sole proprietor and is not associated with any firm (i.e., the broker is the firm) in the same way it restricts an associated salesperson?
choice_a: The prohibition applies identically regardless of whether the licensee is associated with a firm or is a sole proprietor
choice_b: The prohibition in s. 452.14(3)(f) is expressly conditioned on the licensee being "associated with a firm"; a sole proprietor broker who is the firm does not fall within that same conditional language
choice_c: A sole proprietor broker may never accept any compensation directly, without exception
choice_d: The prohibition applies only to sole proprietor brokers, not to associated salespersons
explanation: By its terms, s. 452.14(3)(f) applies "if the licensee is associated with a firm"; a broker who is the firm is not receiving compensation from someone other than "the firm" in the sense the provision addresses.
source_note: hedge: Wis. Stat. 452.14(3)(f) -- the sole-proprietor implication is a reasonable reading of the 'if the licensee is associated with a firm' conditional clause, not a separately spelled-out statutory rule or confirmed by located case law.

question: Under s. 452.14(3)(j), is it a disciplinary violation for a licensee to pay a commission to another person for services performed in violation of ch. 452?
choice_a: No, only the person receiving the improper payment can be disciplined, not the licensee who paid it
choice_b: No, s. 452.14(3)(j) only applies to accepting improper payments, not making them
choice_c: Yes, paying or offering to pay a commission or valuable consideration to any person for acts or services in violation of ch. 452 is grounds for discipline under s. 452.14(3)(j)
choice_d: No, this is a criminal matter only and is not subject to board discipline
explanation: Section 452.14(3)(j) reaches the payor as well as the recipient: paying or offering to pay a commission for acts or services that violate ch. 452 is itself a disciplinary ground.

question: Reading ss. 452.14(3)(f) and 452.14(3)(j) together, which pair of commission-related acts can each expose a licensee to discipline?
choice_a: (f) failing to maintain trust account records, and (j) advertising without firm approval
choice_b: (f) misrepresenting the condition of a property, and (j) failing to complete continuing education
choice_c: (f) discriminating based on a protected class, and (j) using forms not approved by the board
choice_d: (f) accepting compensation from someone other than the licensee's own firm when associated with a firm, and (j) paying or offering to pay compensation to any person for acts performed in violation of ch. 452
explanation: Paragraphs (f) and (j) of s. 452.14(3) are the chapter's two commission-specific disciplinary grounds: improperly accepting compensation, and improperly paying it.

question: Under s. 452.34(1), how is an "unlicensed personal assistant" defined for purposes of ch. 452?
choice_a: An individual employed only to provide services for which a license is not required
choice_b: Any employee of a real estate firm who has not yet passed the salesperson licensing exam
choice_c: A licensed salesperson working under a mentorship or training agreement
choice_d: Any independent contractor retained by a firm to provide marketing services
explanation: Section 452.34(1) defines an unlicensed personal assistant as an individual employed only to provide services that do not require a real estate license.

question: Under s. 452.34(2), before a licensee may use the services of an unlicensed personal assistant, what must the licensee and the firm do regarding the assistant's compensation?
choice_a: Obtain prior written approval from the Real Estate Examining Board for the specific compensation amount
choice_b: Enter into a written agreement with the firm setting forth the assistant's duties, the manner in which the assistant will be compensated, and the responsibilities of the licensee and the firm
choice_c: File the compensation arrangement with the Department of Financial Institutions
choice_d: Nothing -- compensation for unlicensed personal assistants is unregulated under ch. 452
explanation: Section 452.34(2) requires a written agreement with the firm addressing the assistant's duties, compensation method, and each party's responsibilities before the assistant is used.

question: Under s. 452.03(2), is a license required for an individual who performs purely administrative, clerical, or personal services on behalf of and under the direction of a firm or licensee?
choice_a: Yes, any individual performing any task for a firm must be licensed, without exception
choice_b: Yes, unless the individual is a close relative of the licensee
choice_c: No, s. 452.03(2) exempts individuals whose services are limited to those that are purely administrative, clerical, or personal in nature
choice_d: No, but only if the individual is paid on an hourly basis rather than a commission basis
explanation: Section 452.03(2) exempts from licensure individuals whose services for a firm or licensee are limited to purely administrative, clerical, or personal tasks.

question: Under s. 452.03(1), which activities generally require a real estate license in Wisconsin?
choice_a: Only activities involving a transaction over $100,000
choice_b: Only activities performed for compensation exceeding $1,000 per transaction
choice_c: Only activities involving commercial, non-residential property
choice_d: Engaging in or following the business or occupation of, or advertising or holding oneself out as, or acting temporarily or otherwise as, a broker or salesperson
explanation: Section 452.03(1) broadly requires licensure for engaging in, following, advertising, or holding oneself out as a broker or salesperson, without a dollar or property-type threshold.

question: According to the case annotation under s. 452.19 discussing Badger III Ltd. Partnership v. Howard, Needles, Tammen & Bergendoff, why is an agreement to pay a commission to an unlicensed person void, even where the parties route the payment through a properly licensed broker?
choice_a: Because under s. 452.03, an agreement to pay a commission to a person not licensed as a broker is void at its inception, and inserting a licensed broker as a pass-through who performs no actual services does not cure that defect
choice_b: Because the licensed broker in that case failed to sign the agreement
choice_c: Because the commission amount exceeded a statutory cap on referral fees
choice_d: Because the agreement was not filed with the Department of Safety and Professional Services within 30 days
explanation: The annotation explains that a commission agreement with an unlicensed person is void at its inception under s. 452.03, and using a non-participating licensed broker as a conduit does not create a valid co-brokerage arrangement.
source_note: Wis. Stat. 452.19, case annotation citing Badger III Ltd. Partnership v. Howard, Needles, Tammen & Bergendoff, 196 Wis. 2d 891 (Ct. App. 1995)

question: What does s. 452.01(4w) define a "firm" as, for purposes of determining to whom a licensee's commission must be paid under s. 452.19(1m)(b)?
choice_a: Any business entity that employs at least one real estate licensee
choice_b: A licensed individual broker acting as a sole proprietorship or a licensed broker business entity
choice_c: A partnership of two or more licensed salespersons
choice_d: Any entity registered with the Department of Financial Institutions as a real estate company
explanation: Section 452.01(4w) defines "firm" as a licensed individual broker acting as a sole proprietorship, or a licensed broker business entity -- the entity to which associated licensees' compensation must flow under s. 452.19(1m)(b).

question: Under s. 452.01(1o), what does it mean for a licensee to be "associated with a firm" -- a status that triggers the requirement in s. 452.19(1m)(b) that compensation be paid to the firm?
choice_a: To hold an ownership interest of at least 10% in the firm
choice_b: To have closed at least one transaction through the firm in the current calendar year
choice_c: To have been engaged by a firm to provide brokerage services to the firm's clients and customers on behalf of the firm and under the firm's supervision, whether as an employee, as an independent contractor, or both
choice_d: To be listed as an authorized signatory on the firm's trust account
explanation: Section 452.01(1o) defines "associated with a firm" as being engaged by the firm to provide brokerage services to its clients/customers under the firm's supervision, whether as an employee, independent contractor, or both.

question: A firm listing a 1-4 unit residential property wants to accept a "marketing cooperation fee" from a cooperating firm representing the buyer. Under s. 452.19(3)(a), is this kind of fee permitted?
choice_a: Yes, marketing cooperation fees are expressly exempted from the firm-to-firm compensation prohibition
choice_b: Yes, as long as both firms disclose the fee to their respective clients
choice_c: Yes, provided the fee is under $250
choice_d: No -- s. 452.19(3)(a) generally bars a firm from accepting compensation of any kind from another firm in this type of residential transaction, and a marketing cooperation fee is not the narrow referral/finder's fee exception carved out in subd. 3
explanation: Section 452.19(3)(a) prohibits firm-to-firm compensation in 1-4 unit residential transactions except for the referral/finder's fee exception in subd. 3; a marketing cooperation fee does not fit that narrow exception.

question: Under s. 452.19(4)(a), whose signatures are required on the offer to purchase or option to purchase for a seller's agreement to compensate a non-listing firm to be valid?
choice_a: Both the buyer and the seller
choice_b: Only the seller
choice_c: Only the buyer
choice_d: Only the listing firm's designated broker
explanation: Section 452.19(4)(a) requires the agreement to be expressly stated in the fully executed offer or option to purchase and signed by both the buyer and the seller.

question: Under s. 452.19(4)(d), which contractual document (not the offer to purchase itself) must include a statement on whether the seller authorizes disclosure of compensation offered to a firm other than the listing firm?
choice_a: The buyer agency agreement
choice_b: The listing contract
choice_c: The real property condition report
choice_d: The closing disclosure statement
explanation: Section 452.19(4)(d) requires the listing contract to include a statement addressing whether the seller authorizes the listing firm to disclose compensation offered to a non-listing firm.
